input:
Start-up
Before the pump is started, it is essential that a number of preparatory checks are carried out carefully, because a centrifugal pump that is started in the wrong condition can be damaged very quickly. First and foremost, the casing must be completely filled with the liquid that is to be pumped, so that the pump is fully primed; a pump that is started dry will deliver no liquid at all, and the seal faces will run without the cooling and lubrication that the liquid would normally provide, potentially leading to rapid wear. The suction valve should be opened fully, and the discharge valve should be left closed or only partly open, in accordance with whatever the plant procedure for the particular service lays down. The bearing housing should be inspected to confirm that the lubricant is standing at its correct mark and appears clean, and it should also be confirmed that the coupling guard is securely in place and that no tools or loose items have been left near the coupling. Where the design permits, the shaft should be turned by hand to check that it rotates freely, and the suction line should be verified as open along its whole length, with no blind inadvertently left in place and the suction strainer clean. The motor can then be started and the pump allowed to come up to speed, after which the discharge valve is opened gradually while the discharge pressure is watched as it rises towards its normal running value. The seal or gland should be observed for any leakage beyond a slight weep, and the operator should listen carefully for any abnormal noise. If the discharge pressure fails to rise, the pump must be stopped and the cause investigated before any further attempt is made, since running without prime, or running for an extended period against a closed discharge valve, will heat the liquid trapped inside the casing. The start can only be regarded as complete once pressure, leakage, and running sound are all entirely normal and steady.

Normal operation
During normal operation, the pump should be held as closely as possible at its duty flow and head, and the operating point should be kept within the range for which the pump was originally selected. The discharge pressure and the flow should be watched regularly, and any drift in either of them, occurring while valve positions remain unchanged, should be treated as an indication that something somewhere in the pump or in the surrounding system has changed. The suction side deserves particular attention: a falling suction level, a strainer that is gradually blocking, or air being drawn in at a flange will typically manifest itself first as increased noise and vibration, accompanied by an unsteady discharge pressure. It is important to appreciate that cavitation causes real damage to the impeller, and that it is corrected at the suction side, by restoring the level, clearing the strainer, or eliminating the air leak, rather than by adjustment at the discharge valve. The bearing housing should be checked for excessive heat, using the fitted instrument or the back of the hand, and the lubricant level and condition should be verified at the rounds interval that has been established for the plant. The seal or gland should likewise be kept under observation: although a slight weep is perfectly normal for a packed gland, a growing leak, hot running, or a gland that stops weeping altogether should be reported and attended to. The pump should never be run for long periods against a closed or nearly closed discharge valve, because the trapped liquid will heat up and the seals and casing may be damaged as a consequence. A log should be maintained of pressures, temperatures, and any changes in sound or vibration, with the time of each change recorded alongside it, and any departure from normal running should be reported immediately, together with a record of the action that was taken in response, so that the following shift can read the state of the pump from the log rather than relying on memory.

Alarms
The pump is fitted with two alarms, each of which requires a specific response from the operator. No other alarm is raised on this pump.
Low discharge pressure. This alarm indicates that the pump has effectively stopped delivering against the system, which may have happened because prime has been lost, because the suction supply has failed, or because the discharge path is standing open to a level that the pump is unable to hold. The suction supply and the suction level should be checked first of all. If the supply can be restored and the pressure returns to normal, the pump may be kept running and the event should be recorded in the log. If, on the other hand, the pressure does not return, the pump should be stopped, the discharge valve closed, and the event reported; under no circumstances should the pump be restarted until the underlying cause has been identified and the pump has been fully primed again.
High bearing temperature. This alarm indicates that the bearing is running hotter than it should, which may be attributable to a loss or failure of the lubricant, to misalignment, or to a load that falls outside the range for which the pump was selected. The pump should be stopped immediately and the discharge valve closed. The bearing should then be allowed to cool down naturally, without any interference. Once the housing has cooled sufficiently to be handled, the lubricant level and its condition should be checked. The pump must not be restarted until the cause of the overheating has been found and properly corrected, and the alarm, the action taken, and the eventual finding should all be recorded in the log. Restarting a bearing that is still hot, without having established why it became hot, risks converting what was merely a warning into an outright failure of the bearing itself, and very often of the seal that sits behind it as well.

Shutdown
When the pump is to be shut down, it should be brought to a stop broadly in the reverse order of the start-up procedure. The discharge valve should be closed gradually until the flow has stopped completely, bearing in mind that a sudden closure can send a damaging pressure surge back through the discharge line. The motor should then be stopped, and the suction valve closed. As the shaft runs down, it should be watched and listened to carefully, and any rubbing or knocking that is noticed as it slows should be reported and recorded before the pump is left unattended. If the pump is going to stand idle for any length of time, the casing should be drained wherever there is a risk that the liquid left inside it might solidify, attack the casing material, or freeze during cold weather, and the drain should be left in whatever state the plant procedure directs. All pressure within the casing and the connected lines must be relieved before any cover is slackened. Where maintenance work is to be carried out on the pump, it must first be isolated from both the suction and the discharge lines, the motor must be locked so that it cannot be started, and the pump must be proved dead before work begins. The pump should then be handed over to the maintenance crew in precisely that condition, with its state duly recorded in the log. It should be remembered that a pump which has been left filled, pressurised, or free to start cannot be regarded as shut down, regardless of the position of its valves.
target:
Start-up
Prepare the pump and the connected pipework before the motor is started. Fill the casing with the liquid to be pumped until the pump is fully primed. A centrifugal pump started dry delivers no liquid, and the seal faces run without the cooling and lubrication that the liquid provides. Open the suction valve fully. Set the discharge valve closed or partly open, as the plant procedure for the service directs. Inspect the bearing housing and confirm that the lubricant stands at its mark and is clean. Confirm that the coupling guard is in place and that no tools or loose material rest near the coupling. Turn the shaft by hand where the design allows hand turning, and confirm that it turns freely. Confirm that the suction line is open along its whole length, with no blind left in place and the suction strainer clean. Start the motor and let the pump come up to speed. Open the discharge valve gradually and watch the discharge pressure rise to its normal running value. Inspect the seal or gland for leakage beyond a slight weep, and listen for noise beyond the normal running sound. Where discharge pressure does not rise, stop the pump and find the cause before a further start; a pump run without prime, or run for long against a closed discharge valve, heats the liquid trapped in the casing. The start is complete when pressure, leakage, and running sound are all normal and steady, and the pump is left in that state. Keep the area around the pump clear while the start is in progress, and stay at the pump until it has settled into steady running; a fault at start-up shows in the first minutes, and the operator at the pump is the one placed to stop it.

Normal operation
Hold the pump at its duty flow and head, and keep the operating point inside the range the pump was selected for. Watch the discharge pressure and the flow, and treat a drift in either, at unchanged valve positions, as a sign that something in the pump or in the system around it has changed. Keep the suction side under watch: a falling suction level, a blocking strainer, or air drawn in at a flange shows first as noise and vibration, with the discharge pressure unsteady. Cavitation damages the impeller and is corrected at the suction side, by restoring the level, clearing the strainer, or stopping the air leak; it is not corrected at the discharge valve. Check the bearing housing for heat by the fitted instrument or by hand, and check the lubricant level and condition at the rounds interval set for the plant. Watch the seal or gland: a slight weep is normal for a packed gland, while a growing leak, hot running, or a gland that stops weeping altogether is reported and seen to. Do not run the pump for long against a closed or nearly closed discharge valve; the trapped liquid heats, and the seals and casing are damaged by the heat. Keep a log of pressures, temperatures, and every change in sound or vibration, with the time of the change noted against it. Report departures from normal running at once, and record what was done in response, so that the next shift reads the state of the pump from the log and not from memory. Where the pump runs in parallel with a second pump on the same service, watch the sharing of the flow between the two as well; a drift in one machine moves load onto the other, and the pair is read together rather than as two separate machines.

Alarms
Two alarms are fitted to this pump, and each alarm has its operator action. No other alarm is raised on the pump.
Low discharge pressure. The alarm means that the pump has stopped delivering against the system: prime has been lost, the suction supply has failed, or the discharge path stands open to a level the pump cannot hold. Check the suction supply and the suction level first. Where the supply is restored and the pressure returns, keep the pump running and log the event. Where the pressure does not return, stop the pump, close the discharge valve, and report the event; do not restart until the cause has been found and the pump has been primed again.
High bearing temperature. The alarm means that the bearing is running hot, from loss or failure of the lubricant, from misalignment, or from a load outside the range the pump was selected for. Stop the pump at once and close the discharge valve. Let the bearing cool without interference. When the housing can be handled, check the lubricant level and its condition. Do not restart the pump until the cause of the heating has been found and corrected, and record the alarm, the action taken, and the finding in the log. A hot bearing restarted without a finding converts a warning into a failure of the bearing, and commonly of the seal behind it. An alarm that returns after its cause has been corrected is treated as a new event and not as a nuisance: the finding from the earlier event is re-opened, and the pump is not returned to unattended running until the repeat has been explained.

Shutdown
Bring the pump to a stop in the reverse order of the start. Close the discharge valve gradually until the flow stops; a sudden closure sends a pressure surge back through the discharge line. Stop the motor. Close the suction valve. Watch the shaft run down and listen for rubbing or knocking as it slows; a noise on rundown is reported and recorded before the pump is left. Where the pump will stand idle, drain the casing if the liquid left in it could solidify, attack the casing, or freeze in cold weather, and leave the drain in the state the plant procedure directs. Relieve the pressure in the casing and in the connected lines before any cover is slackened. Where work is to be done on the pump, isolate it from the suction and discharge lines, lock the motor against starting, and prove the pump dead before the work begins. Hand the pump over to the maintenance crew in that state, with the state recorded in the log. A pump left filled, pressurised, or free to start is not shut down, whatever the position of its valves. Record the shutdown in the log with the reason for it, planned or unplanned, and the state in which the pump is left, so that the next start begins from a known state rather than from an inspection made under time pressure.
